title: Chapter 214 – The Free Gift
html:
[Terrace Four – Lan Xiu]

Lan Xiu learns to walk again on the sixth day, and the first thing she does with her new legs is fall down.

She does it on purpose. That is the thing she will remember, years from now, when the stone in her hips has softened to nothing and she can run for a mile without losing her breath. She stands at the lip of the Quay with one hand on the Cartographer's shoulder and the other on the cold gray flank of a sleeping Keeper, and she lets go of both, and takes one step into the dust. Her left leg holds. Her right leg, which has been stone to the knee for ten days, gives a long slow grind like a gate on a rusty hinge, and she goes down on her palms and her chin and lies there laughing, soundlessly, with her cheek against the Terrace.

Well done, says the Cartographer, in her head.

She has stopped finding it strange. That is another thing she will remember. The warm, rumpled voice in the quiet of her mind, the old man's sigh, the faint rasp of a pen across skin. Hua's mark is a thread that runs from the heavy man's bandaged hand to the Warden's palm and out, in some way she doesn't understand, to the whole Terrace; and on the third day, when she woke with a headache and a fear of her own thoughts, he had told her that it was only a matter of leaving the door open. You needn't speak. You need only not mind being heard.

She minds. She minds terribly. But she is fifteen, and alive, and the Silent Terrace has taken everything else she thought she knew about being a person, so she lets him listen.

She pushes herself up on her knees.

Again, she thinks.

Again, he agrees, and she can hear the smile.

---

They have fallen into a rhythm, the three of them, the old man and the girl and the child.

In the morning the Cartographer feeds the stove and Lan Xiu practices her legs, and Mo Yan sits on the step of the shed with the white bell in her lap and does not speak. That is the part that frightens Lan Xiu most. The child has been quiet since the others left. Not sullen; not frightened. Simply quiet, as a pond is quiet when the wind drops. She holds the white bell in both hands and rocks it a little, as one rocks a sleeping infant, and her lips move slightly, and sometimes she smiles at nothing.

In the afternoon Lan Xiu goes down to the Quay and sits among her stone sisters.

She tells them about the day. She tells them what the Cartographer said, and what she ate, and the joke Mo Yan made about the lid on the table. She tells them that she is not afraid. She tells them it is only a little while, and that someone is coming back with a song. She tells them every word as though they were listening, because the first of her teachers once told her that stone remembers everything said in front of it, and she has decided that if she is wrong, there is no harm.

Nobody answers. But on the fourth afternoon, when she finishes and turns to go, she sees that the nearest of them, a tall girl named Pei who always laughed at her accent, has moved. Not much. A hair. The stone fingers on the lifted hand have curled in toward the palm, as though in the act of making a fist.

She stands very still for a long time.

Then she goes up the Quay at a limping run to find the Cartographer.

---

He is not in the shed. He is in the arch.

He sits on the stone bench, under the list of names, with a long white scroll unrolled on his knees and a pen in his bandaged hand. His broad face is grave. When she appears in the doorway he looks up, and rubs his eyes, and she sees that he has been crying.

You were right, he says, before she can speak. They are moving.

Pei's hand.

Pei, and the boy in the second row. And one of the older Keepers by the north wall. He lays the pen across the scroll. It began last night. I thought it was a trick of the light. I counted, to be sure. The kind, tired mouth twists. Seventeen so far.

That's good. Isn't it?

It would be.

He holds out the scroll.

It is a map. She knows by now what his maps look like, the fine brown lines, the little careful cross-strokes, the absent-minded sketches in the margins of cats and kettles. This one is different. It is a single great spiral, drawn from the outside in, with each turn tighter than the last, and at its center there is a black circle, and in the circle there is a name.

Mo Yan.

It is written in a thin upright hand. Beneath it is the same name again, and again, a hundred times, a thousand, in smaller and smaller characters, until the lines blur into a gray haze. She can see, now, that the haze is not ink. It is the pen itself, the way it has been pressed into the skin of the map, so deeply that it has torn through in places.

That is Orrin's hand, the Cartographer says. I would know it anywhere. I taught him to make that stroke. A shuddering breath. But I did not teach him to do this. I do not think he did it. I think he was made to.

When?

The ink is wet. He lays two fingers on the haze. When he lifts them, she sees a faint bright smear. Four days. Perhaps five. It has been written continuously since the night the child spoke her mother's name.

Her mother's name.

She said "Mama," he says gently. On the Third Terrace, at the furnace. I did not hear it. But the Ferryman did, and the bell did, and the bell is an old thing and tells everything it knows. He rubs his eyes. And she said it again at the Quay, when she paid.

She did not say it. She lost it.

That is how it speaks. The Cartographer's voice is very low. The Bloom does not take what is given. It takes what is left behind. And a name that has just been paid is a very large thing to leave.

---

They tell Mo Yan together.

She listens without moving, sitting on the shed step with the white bell in her lap. She does not cry. She does not argue. When the Cartographer has finished, and Lan Xiu has finished, and the dust has settled over the long gray quiet of the Terrace, the child lifts her face and looks at them with an expression Lan Xiu has never seen on a child.

It is not fear. It is not courage either. It is the grave, clear, tired look of someone who has just been told the weather.

"So it wants me," says Mo Yan.

I believe so, the Cartographer says.

"Because I paid."

Because you paid, and you did not run, and you are nine. He sits on the step beside her, heavily, with a creak of knees. Nine is a number the Seam likes. The Founders chose it, long ago, and it has remained.

"And Sera?"

His hand stills.

I do not know, he says.

"She's not lying to me."

I did not say she was.

"She's not." Mo Yan's small hands tighten on the bell. "I can hear her. She says things, and they're true. She says she's tired. She says she's frightened. She says there's someone with her, and he's not nice, and she doesn't know what he wants." Her chin lifts. "She says I'm the first person who's said 'I'm here' in six hundred years."

That is not the same as being safe.

"I know."

Then you understand.

"I understand that I'm the only one she's got." The child's voice does not shake. "I'm not going to put her down."

For a long time, nobody speaks.

Lan Xiu looks at the old man. His face is wet. He looks, she thinks, like a man who has just been handed his own life and told to carry it down a flight of stairs.

There is a way, he says at last. I do not like it.

"Tell me."

The Wall. He lifts his bandaged hand. The Hundred Stairs run down from this Terrace to the Azure Cloud Sect, and the Sect's road to the Wall. It is nine days' walk for a man, perhaps twelve for a child. There is a tower there. A man in the tower is a keystone, and a keystone holds the Seam steady. If you were near him, the Bloom's reach would be dampened. Perhaps even stopped.

"Wenyuan," Mo Yan says.

Yes.

"But the Road's closed above us. Jian said. If I go down, I can't come up."

The Road above is closed, the Cartographer agrees. The Road below is open. You may go as far as you like, and come back, and go again. He smiles, a tired, crooked smile. It was only the going up that the Founders thought fit to lock.

Mo Yan studies him, with her black unflinching eyes.

"You'll come."

I will carry the lid, he says. And the maps. And Lan Xiu, if she tires.

"Lan Xiu's legs are fine," says Lan Xiu, indignantly, in her head, and the old man laughs out loud, a rusty, startled laugh, and the Terrace takes it, as it takes everything, and swallows the sound without a trace.

---

On the sixth night, the Cartographer shows her the book.

It is a small, flat, brown thing, no bigger than her hand, bound in some kind of dark leather that has gone soft at the corners. He takes it from the inside of his cloak, where he has kept it, and lays it on the table between them, beside the lid of dark metal, and does not open it. The stove is low. Mo Yan has gone to sleep on the bench, curled around the white bell, and Lan Xiu sits across from the old man with a cup of bitter tea going cold in her hands.

This is the only copy, he says. I wrote it in the first year. I have carried it ever since.

What is it?

The song. He rubs his eyes. The Founders called it the Cradle. It is the thing the Keepers sang, in the first days, when they chose the Silence. They sang it so that those who followed might know the way back. The kind, tired mouth curves. It is not long. Eleven lines. It is a lullaby, really, though a strange one. It was meant to be sung by a person who has paid.

Like Mo Yan.

Like you. He pushes the book across the table. Like anyone who has been where the sleepers are. The words are not a spell. They are a promise. They say: we remember you, we have not gone, the door is open. A Keeper who hears them knows that someone has come. He lays one broad finger on the cover. If you wake the others, it will be by this.

Lan Xiu does not touch the book.

You should keep it, she says. You know it better.

I know it too well. His smile is lopsided. A man who has sung a thing for two hundred years begins to hear it in his sleep. It becomes a kind of wallpaper. You will hear it fresh. That is a gift.

I am fifteen.

You are a girl who woke from stone with her mind and her heart, and who sat up at night to tell her sisters the news. He is looking at her with such gentle, steady regard that she has to look away. I have watched you for six days. I do not know many people who would have done that.

She turns the cup in her hands.

What if I get it wrong?

Then you will try again. He rubs his eyes. That is what the Terrace is for. It is not a place of perfect things. It is a place where people stay.

She picks up the book.

It is warm from his body. The leather is soft, the pages thin and faintly gritty with age. She opens it to the first leaf and finds a single line, in a small neat hand she knows from a hundred maps:

For whoever comes. Do not be afraid. It is only a song.

She closes it again, quickly, because her eyes have begun to sting.

Thank you, she says.

Do not thank me yet. The Cartographer reaches over and tucks the book into the bundle by the door, between the bread and the lid. Keep it dry. Keep it close. And if anything should happen to me—

Nothing will happen to you.

—if anything should happen, he says, as kindly as if she had not spoken, do not stay to look. A gift that cannot be taken is worth more than a gift that cannot be left.

She does not know what he means. She nods anyway.

Outside the shed, in the dark, the Silent Terrace turns slowly toward morning. And somewhere deep in the sleeping stone, so faintly that neither of them hears it, seventeen Keepers shift their weight from one foot to the other.

---

They leave at dusk on the seventh day.

Lan Xiu carries the bundle. The Cartographer has packed it with his usual care: three loaves of flat bread, a skin of water, the lid of dark metal, a dozen maps rolled in oilcloth, and a small, flat, brown book, which he does not explain. Mo Yan walks between them with the white bell tucked into her cloak. Lan Xiu keeps one hand on the child's shoulder. She does not say why. She suspects the child knows.

At the edge of the Quay, they stop.

Lan Xiu looks back. She cannot help it. The Terrace lies behind them in the blue light, vast and quiet and strange, the sleeping Keepers standing in their rows, the great arch, the shed with its small gold window. The five stone pupils on the lip of the Quay are only shapes. She whispers their names, one by one, in her mind.

Pei. Hu. Anlan. Fan. Shu.

We will come back, she tells them.

On the nearest, Pei's stone fist loosens, very slowly, and opens, palm outward, in the dusk.

Lan Xiu turns away before she can cry.

The Hundred Stairs begin at the foot of the Quay, a narrow white flight cut into the cliff, so steep that the first step vanishes into mist. She has climbed them once. She doesn't remember the climb. It was a day of cold and cloud and Elder Ye's brisk voice calling the pace, and she had been proud, then, to be one of seven.

Now, says the Cartographer, and sets his foot on the top stair.

Nothing happens.

Lan Xiu lets out her breath. She hadn't known she was holding it. She takes a step, and another, with Mo Yan's small hand in hers. The stone is cold and damp. The mist rises round their ankles. Behind them, the Silent Terrace draws back, little by little, into the blue, until the Quay is only a gray line, and the arch is a smudge, and the stove-light in the Cartographer's shed is a single faint star.

She is starting to think it might be easy.

It is Mo Yan who stops.

---

She stops on the thirty-first step.

It happens suddenly: one moment the child is walking, the next she is standing quite still, with her head cocked, like a bird that has heard a sound in the grass. Her hand has gone slack in Lan Xiu's. Her face is perfectly calm.

"Mo Yan?"

The child does not answer.

What is it? the Cartographer says, from above.

I don't know. She's—

"Mama," says Mo Yan.

The word comes out of her in a small clear voice, and the Terrace behind them, the Terrace that has not carried a sound in six hundred years, gives it back.

It rolls down the cliff face like a thrown stone. It is quiet and bright and perfectly clear. It echoes once, twice, three times, off the white rock, and every echo is a little louder than the last, and Lan Xiu feels the hair stand up along her arms.

Mo Yan, thinks the Cartographer, urgently. Child. Do not speak.

"Mama," says Mo Yan again.

And from the Silent Terrace, from the long quiet rows of the four hundred sleepers, from the open mouths of the stone Keepers who gave themselves to the wall against the Bloom's scream, an answer comes.

It is a woman's voice.

It is a low, warm, tired voice, with a rasp in it, as of someone who has been up all night with a sick child. It does not come from one place. It comes from all of them, four hundred mouths in a hundred different pitches, layered one upon another until the sound is a single great chord, as gentle as a hand on a forehead.

Mo Yan, it says. Little one. Come here.

Lan Xiu's knees go weak.

She has never heard it before. She knows, with a certainty that has nothing to do with knowing, that it is the voice Mo Yan lost. It is her mother's. It is the voice that said her name in the dark, on the nights when the cart-house was cold. It is the voice that told her to go to sleep, and that someone would come.

I've been looking for you, it says. I've been looking such a long time.

Mo Yan takes a step up the stairs.

---

"No!" Lan Xiu gasps.

She catches the child by the shoulder. She cannot help it; she doesn't think. She whirls her around, and Mo Yan's face is white and wet and shining, and her eyes are enormous, and she is looking through Lan Xiu at the dusk behind her.

"That's my mama," Mo Yan whispers.

It isn't.

"She's calling me."

It isn't, Mo Yan. It's the Bloom. It's using your mother's voice to—

"Then why does it sound so true?"

Because it is. The Cartographer has come down the stairs, heavily, and put himself between the child and the Terrace, his gray cloak spread like a wall. Child, listen. It is true. Everything it says is true. It has found your mother's voice in the dark of your own mind, and it is using the kindest words you ever heard. That is its whole art.

"She says she's been looking for me."

Yes.

"She says she wants to give it back." Mo Yan swallows. "My name. Her name. She says it's free. She says it doesn't cost anything."

It doesn't, says the Cartographer.

Lan Xiu stares at him.

That is how you know, he says, very softly. He is holding Mo Yan's gaze, steadily, with the bleary kind eyes of a man who has made a great many mistakes and would like not to make another. Veyra told Hua. I heard her, through the mark. A real voice costs. The Ferryman's cost him his life. Sera's cost her three years. Yours cost your mother's name. He puts his hand on her small shoulder. This one costs nothing. It asks nothing. It simply offers.

"But I want it."

I know.

"I want it so much."

I know, little one. So do I.

The great gentle chord is rising. It is no longer a voice but a tide, four hundred mothers calling four hundred children, and the stairs are shaking under their feet. Lan Xiu feels it in her teeth. She feels the Terrace gathering itself, like a lung before a cry.

It's going to scream, she thinks. If she answers, it's going to scream.

It is, says the Cartographer. It has been waiting six hundred years for a child to say yes.

He kneels.

It takes him a long time. He lowers himself onto the step with a creak of knees and a grunt, and takes Mo Yan's face between his two hands, the bandaged and the bare. His eyes are full of tears. He smiles.

I drew you a map once, he says, and it was wrong. I drew the Road as a spiral. I drew it climbing. I did not know it also falls. He kisses her forehead. Go down, little one. Go down, and do not look back, and do not answer, and do not stop until you reach the tower. Lan Xiu will go with you. You will be safe.

"Cartographer—"

It is all right. He rises, slowly, with the stiffness of an old man, and turns to face the Terrace. I have one thing left that I can do. I am rather good at it. I have had two hundred years of practice.

What? Lan Xiu thinks. What are you doing?

I am going to make a noise, says the Cartographer.

---

She understands too late.

He walks up the stairs. He does not hurry. He climbs the thirty-one steps he has just come down, one by one, with his gray cloak dragging on the stone and his bandaged hand held against his chest, and the great gentle chord parts for him as water parts for a stone. He reaches the Quay. He stands in the dusk, on the lip, between the five stone pupils and the four hundred sleepers, and he lifts his head.

And he sings.

It is not a song. It is not even a tune. It is one note, low and rough and enormous, torn from the bottom of a chest that has not drawn a full breath in two hundred years. It is the first sound that has been made aloud on the Silent Terrace since the Keepers chose their silence, and it goes out across the dust like a bell, and it does not stop.

The Terrace takes it.

Lan Xiu sees it happen. She sees the dust rise. She sees the stone in his hands go gray, then paler, then white, creeping up his wrists, up his arms, into the shoulders of his gray cloak. He does not falter. The note goes on, and on, and as it goes the great gentle chord of the Bloom fractures and collapses, because it cannot compete with a thing that is real, a thing that has paid and is paying, a voice with a cost on it that anyone could hear.

Go, says the Cartographer's last thought, a faint warm breath in her mind. Go. Run. Hua—tell Hua—

The thought breaks off.

The note goes on a moment longer, and then it stops. The Quay is silent. The Terrace is silent. Down the white stair, in the mist, a girl of fifteen has a small hand clamped in both of hers and is running, running, running, with her heart in her throat, and she does not look back.

She does not need to.

In the dusk behind them, at the edge of the Quay, a heavy man in a gray cloak stands with his head thrown back and his mouth open on a single endless note. His hands are raised. He is rubbing his eyes. He will go on rubbing them, in stone, for as long as there is a stone to rub them in.

And in the arch above him, on the great list of the sleeping, the carver's chisel that has lain idle for six hundred years begins, very softly, to move.
